analysis.one_liner: Bans Medicare pharmacy middlemen from pocketing hidden drug-price spreads and secret manufacturer fees.
analysis.headline: The House Energy and Commerce Committee approved the bill unanimously, 46 to 0, but the full House never voted on it before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets pharmacy benefit managers, the middleman companies that decide which drugs Medicare plans cover and how much pharmacies get paid. It would bar these companies from making money off anything but a flat, disclosed service fee, stop them from charging Medicare plans more than they pay the pharmacy that fills the prescription, require them to pay independent pharmacies at least what they pay their own pharmacies, and publicly report how much they keep from the rebates drug makers pay them. It was approved unanimously by the House committee with jurisdiction but never came to a vote in the full House.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and community pharmacies. The bill would cut off middleman income based on drug prices, which is the revenue that drives higher list prices, and it would stop pay-to-affiliated-pharmacy favoritism that pushes independent drugstores out of Medicare networks.

how_it_helps.text: Bars Medicare pharmacy benefit managers from earning income on covered drugs from any source other than flat, written service fees, and those fees cannot be based on drug prices or on discounts and rebates the manager receives [S3] [S2].
Stops managers from charging the Medicare plan more for a drug's cost and dispensing than they actually pay the pharmacy, ending spread pricing inside Medicare [S3] [S2].
Requires managers to pay independent network pharmacies at least as much as they pay their own affiliated pharmacies, removing a structural disadvantage for local drugstores [S3] [S2].

Requires public reporting of how much managers receive in manufacturer rebates and fees and how much of it they keep rather than pass through to plans, and adds the manager to the conflict-of-interest rules for Medicare drug coverage [S3] [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The large pharmacy benefit manager companies, which would lose revenue from price-based fees, spread pricing, and manufacturer rebates and fees they currently keep, and would face disgorgement of amounts collected in violation of the rules.

drawbacks.text: Flat fee-only compensation is untested at scale in Medicare; if the fees plans must pay managers to make up for lost rebate income are large, some savings could be offset by higher plan premiums, and the bill does not cap those fees [S3].

The transparency section keeps trade secrets confidential and publishes rebate data only in aggregate, without identifying specific plans, drugs, or rebate amounts, which limits how much patients can actually see about why their drug is priced the way it is [S3].
The bill covers only Medicare drug plans, not employer and commercial coverage, where most working-age Americans get their pharmacy benefits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provisions strike directly at how middleman companies make money on Medicare drugs, and the independent pharmacies that serve many Medicare patients gain a level payment floor. The main honest concerns are that flat fees could partly shift costs into premiums and that the coverage is limited to Medicare rather than the whole market. On balance the benefits to patients and pharmacies outweigh the design limits.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee with jurisdiction approved it unanimously in December 2023, but House leadership never brought it to the floor for a vote, and near the end of the Congress it was referred back to a subcommittee, where it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Introduced April 26, 2023 by Rep. Buddy Carter with three original cosponsors from both parties, and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees [S5] [S3].
The Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee approved it by voice vote on November 15, 2023, and the full committee ordered it reported, as amended, 46 to 0 on December 6, 2023 [S5].

After that vote, the bill never received floor action in the House; on December 17, 2024 it was referred back to the Subcommittee on Health, and the Congress ended January 3, 2025 without a vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large pharmacy benefit manager companies, which keep their price-based fee income, spread pricing, and rebate retention in Medicare for at least another Congress, since no version of these rules became law.

for.name: Rep. Earl L. "Buddy" Carter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed it through the Health Subcommittee, which approved it by voice vote.

for.name: Energy and Commerce Committee (full committee)
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported, as amended, on a 46-0 vote on December 6, 2023.

for.name: Lisa Blunt Rochester, Nicole Malliotakis, and Jake Auchincloss
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as original cosponsors at introduction, alongside 42 more cosponsors drawn from both parties (19 House Democrats and 26 House Republicans in total).

for.name: Independent community pharmacies
for.role: Network pharmacies disadvantaged by spread pricing and affiliated-pharmacy favoritism
for.what_they_did: Publicly supported PBM payment and transparency reform, which this bill provides.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker's office, controls the House floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the committee-approved bill for a vote by the full House in the remainder of the 118th Congress.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit manager companies
against.role: Large Medicare PBM operators (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
against.what_they_did: Lobbied heavily against restrictions on spread pricing and price-based fees, the exact practices this bill bans.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan at every recorded step: 45 cosponsors split 19 Democrats and 26 Republicans, the original four sponsors included two of each party, and the committee reported it 46-0; the decisive block was the absence of a floor vote, not a partisan roll call.

industries.note: The bill bans the core ways PBMs make money in Medicare: fees tied to drug prices, spread pricing between what plans pay and what pharmacies receive, and keeping manufacturer rebates and fees. Their interest in this bill runs directly against patients' drug costs and pharmacy payment levels.

The bill guarantees pharmacies in Medicare networks reimbursement at least equal to what PBM-affiliated pharmacies get, protecting independent drugstores from being underpaid while their PBM competitors are paid more.

Manufacturers keep paying the rebate system itself, but the aggregate reporting of rebates and fees managers keep would expose how much of manufacturers' rebate spending never reaches patients, adding pressure they have avoided.
